questions.q: What is the key advantage of ADLS Gen2 over plain Azure Blob Storage for big data workloads?
options: ADLS Gen2 adds a hierarchical namespace on top of Blob Storage, letting directories and files be renamed or moved as atomic operations, which big data engines like Spark rely on for efficient, POSIX-like file operations
ADLS Gen2 is a completely separate storage product with no relation to Blob Storage
ADLS Gen2 only supports storing CSV files, not other formats
Blob Storage is more expensive than ADLS Gen2 for identical workloads
questions.explain: ADLS Gen2 is Blob Storage with a hierarchical namespace layered on top; that namespace makes directory operations like rename and delete atomic and fast instead of requiring a costly rewrite of every object under a flat key prefix, which is exactly what distributed compute engines need.

questions.q: What does 'hierarchical namespace' mean when enabled on a storage account?
options: It means the storage account can only be accessed by users with hierarchical (tiered) permissions

The storage account organizes objects into an actual directory tree (folders containing files and subfolders) instead of treating every object as a flat key in one namespace, which speeds up operations like listing or renaming a directory
It means data is automatically organized by date, with no user control
It refers to a naming convention with no effect on performance
questions.explain: Without a hierarchical namespace, 'folders' are just a naming convention baked into flat object keys, so renaming a folder means rewriting every object's key; with it enabled, directories are real structural entities, making those operations fast and atomic.

questions.q: What is the difference between RBAC and ACLs when securing an ADLS Gen2 data lake?
options: RBAC and ACLs are two names for the exact same permission model in Azure
ACLs can only deny access, never grant it

RBAC (role-based access control) grants broad, role-based permissions typically at the storage account or container level; ACLs (access control lists) grant fine-grained permissions on individual directories and files, similar to POSIX file permissions
RBAC is only used for Blob Storage, and ACLs are only used for SQL Server
questions.explain: RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Reader apply broadly and are managed through Azure AD; ACLs let you get much more granular, controlling read/write/execute permissions on a specific folder or file the way traditional Unix file permissions do.

questions.q: In a Bronze/Silver/Gold (medallion) architecture, what distinguishes the Bronze layer from the other two?
options: Bronze holds only the final, business-ready aggregated data
Bronze is where all personally identifiable information is permanently deleted
Bronze data is always stored in row-level relational format, never in files
Bronze holds raw, unmodified data exactly as it was ingested from the source, preserving a full historical record before any cleaning or transformation happens
questions.explain: Keeping Bronze as an untouched copy of the source data means you always have a reliable point to reprocess from if a downstream transformation had a bug, without needing to re-pull from the original source system.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a Python list and a dictionary?
options: A list stores an ordered sequence of values accessed by numeric index; a dictionary stores key-value pairs accessed by an arbitrary (often string) key
A list can only store numbers, while a dictionary can store any type
A dictionary is always faster to iterate over in order than a list
Lists are immutable in Python, but dictionaries are mutable
questions.explain: A list is positional — you get an element by its integer position in the sequence — while a dictionary is associative, letting you look up a value directly by a meaningful key like a column name or an ID, without scanning the whole structure.

questions.q: Why use a `try`/`except` block when reading a file or calling an external API in a data pipeline script?
options: It automatically retries the operation an unlimited number of times
It lets the script catch and handle an expected failure (like a missing file or a network timeout) gracefully, instead of the whole program crashing with an unhandled exception
It prevents the code inside `try` from ever raising an exception
It is required syntax for every Python function, even ones that can't fail
questions.explain: External resources like files and APIs fail in predictable ways — a missing file, a timeout, a bad response — and try/except lets you anticipate those specific failures and respond deliberately (log it, retry, skip the record) rather than letting the whole script die.

questions.q: What is a pandas DataFrame?
options: A file format for storing data on disk, like CSV or Parquet
A single column of numeric data with no row labels
An in-memory, two-dimensional labeled data structure (rows and named columns) that supports vectorized operations, filtering, and aggregation, similar to a spreadsheet or SQL table
A wrapper around a live SQL Server connection with no local data
questions.explain: A DataFrame lives in memory as labeled rows and columns, and its methods (filter, groupby, merge) operate on whole columns at once using vectorized operations under the hood, which is why pandas code is both concise and fast compared to row-by-row Python loops.

questions.q: When calling a REST API from Python to pull data for a pipeline, what does the HTTP status code returned in the response tell you?
options: The status code always equals the number of records returned
Status codes are optional metadata that pipelines can safely ignore
A status code of 404 means the server is currently overloaded and will succeed if retried immediately
Whether the request succeeded, failed, or needs authentication/retry — for example 200 means success, 401 means unauthorized, and 429 means you're being rate-limited
questions.explain: Checking the status code lets a pipeline branch its behavior correctly — treating a 200 as data to process, a 401 as a credentials problem to fix, and a 429 as a signal to back off and retry later rather than hammering the API.

questions.q: Why would a data engineer use a library like `pyodbc` or `sqlalchemy` in a Python ETL script?
options: To open a connection to a SQL database and execute queries or load data directly from Python, bridging file-based or API-based data with a relational database
To compress CSV files before uploading them to blob storage
To convert Python scripts into standalone executable files
To visualize data as charts within a Jupyter notebook
questions.explain: These libraries provide the database driver and connection-handling code needed to run SQL from Python, which is how a script pulls source data out of a database or writes transformed results back into one as part of an ETL job.

questions.q: What roles do the Driver and the Executors play in a Spark application?
options: The Driver runs the main program, builds the execution plan, and coordinates work; the Executors are worker processes distributed across the cluster that actually run the tasks and hold data in memory
The Driver stores all the data; Executors only log errors
Executors coordinate the cluster; the Driver just displays results
There is only ever one process total in a Spark job, regardless of cluster size
questions.explain: The Driver is the coordinator — it translates your code into a physical plan and hands out tasks; the Executors are the actual workers spread across cluster nodes that run those tasks in parallel and cache data, which is where Spark's distributed speed comes from.

questions.q: What does 'lazy evaluation' mean in Spark?
options: Spark evaluates every line of code the moment it's written, with no plan optimization
Lazy evaluation means Spark jobs run slower than eager evaluation always

Transformations like `filter` or `select` are not executed immediately — Spark builds up a logical execution plan and only actually runs the computation when an action (like `count` or `write`) triggers it
It refers to Spark automatically caching every DataFrame in memory
questions.explain: By waiting to run anything until an action is called, Spark can look at the whole chain of transformations and optimize the plan — combining steps, pushing filters earlier, skipping unnecessary work — rather than executing each step naively as it's written.

questions.q: What is the difference between a transformation and an action in Spark?
options: Transformations always run on the driver; actions always run on executors
Actions can be chained lazily, while transformations execute immediately
There is no meaningful distinction; the terms are interchangeable

A transformation (like `map` or `filter`) returns a new, lazily-evaluated DataFrame/RDD without triggering computation; an action (like `collect` or `count`) actually triggers execution of the built-up plan and returns a result
questions.explain: This split is what makes lazy evaluation possible: transformations just describe what should happen and build up a plan, while an action is the trigger that actually forces Spark to execute that plan and produce a concrete result.

questions.q: Why does the number of partitions in a Spark DataFrame matter for performance?
options: Partitions determine how the data is split up and processed in parallel across executor cores — too few partitions underutilizes the cluster, while too many creates excessive scheduling overhead
Partitions determine the file format the data is saved in
Increasing partitions always guarantees faster job completion with no downside
Partitions only matter for streaming jobs, not for batch jobs
questions.explain: Each partition is processed by one task on one core, so too few partitions leaves cores idle while a handful of tasks do all the work, and too many partitions creates so much task-scheduling overhead that the coordination cost outweighs the parallelism benefit — the right number balances the two.

questions.q: What is the difference between PySpark's `filter()` and `where()` methods?
options: filter() removes columns, while where() removes rows
They are functionally identical — `where()` is simply an alias for `filter()` provided for users more familiar with SQL syntax
where() can only accept SQL string expressions, and filter() cannot
filter() executes immediately, while where() is deferred until a write
questions.explain: PySpark provides `where()` purely as a familiar alias so SQL-minded users feel at home, but under the hood it calls the exact same code path as `filter()` and behaves identically.

questions.q: What does `withColumn()` do in a PySpark DataFrame?
options: It permanently deletes a column from the underlying data source
It returns a new DataFrame with a column added or an existing column replaced, based on an expression you provide
It renames every column in the DataFrame at once
It merges two DataFrames by matching column names
questions.explain: Because DataFrames are immutable, withColumn doesn't modify anything in place — it returns a brand-new DataFrame that has the specified column either newly added or overwritten with the result of your expression.

questions.q: When you call `.groupBy('region').sum('sales')` in PySpark, what is actually happening?
options: Every row is duplicated once per region in the dataset
The DataFrame is sorted by region with no aggregation applied
groupBy immediately writes the grouped result to disk
Rows are grouped into buckets by the value in the `region` column, and within each bucket the `sales` values are summed, producing one output row per distinct region
questions.explain: groupBy partitions the rows conceptually into one bucket per distinct value of the grouping column, and the aggregate function you chain onto it — here sum — is then computed independently within each bucket, collapsing many rows into one summary row per group.

questions.q: In a PySpark join, what typically causes a shuffle across the cluster?
options: Rows from both DataFrames that don't already live on the same partition or node must be moved (shuffled) across the network so matching keys end up together for the join to happen
Joins in Spark never require moving data between nodes
Shuffling only occurs when joining a DataFrame to itself
Shuffle only happens if the join uses an inner join, never an outer join
questions.explain: For two rows to be joined on a key, they need to be co-located on the same executor at the same time; if matching keys started out on different nodes, Spark has to physically move (shuffle) data across the network to bring them together, which is often the most expensive part of a join.

questions.q: What problem do window functions (like `row_number()` over a partition) solve that a plain `groupBy` cannot?
options: Window functions can only be used with streaming DataFrames, never batch

They let you compute a value (like a rank or running total) for each row while still having access to values from other rows in the same group, without collapsing multiple rows into one aggregated row
They eliminate the need for any `partitionBy` or `orderBy` clause
Window functions replace joins entirely for combining two DataFrames
questions.explain: A groupBy aggregation reduces each group down to one output row, losing the individual rows; a window function instead keeps every original row while adding a computed value derived from its group, which is exactly what you need for things like ranking each transaction within a customer's history.

questions.q: Why is it important to explicitly handle nulls (e.g. with `.na.fill()` or `.dropna()`) before running aggregations in PySpark?
options: PySpark aggregation functions throw a hard error whenever a null is present, so handling isn't optional
Nulls are automatically converted to zero by every PySpark function
Nulls can silently skew or exclude rows from calculations like averages and sums, so leaving them unhandled can produce misleading results without raising any error
Null handling is only relevant when writing to Parquet, not to Delta or CSV
questions.explain: Most aggregate functions quietly skip null values rather than erroring, which means an average or count can look perfectly valid while actually being computed over fewer rows than you expect — deciding deliberately how to treat nulls avoids that silent distortion.

questions.q: Why would you partition a PySpark DataFrame by a column (like `date`) when writing it out?
options: Partitioning the output guarantees the data is fully deduplicated
Writing with partitioning always produces a single output file
Partitioning on write has no effect on later read performance
It organizes the output into separate subfolders by that column's value, so downstream queries that filter on that column can skip reading irrelevant files entirely (partition pruning)
questions.explain: When files are physically laid out in date=2024-01-01/ style subfolders, a later query filtering on that date can skip scanning every other folder entirely, which is dramatically faster than reading the whole dataset and filtering afterward.
